options.misconception: The armor, scepter, and crown present a king, not a merchant — the portrait is about royal power.
options.text: As a merchant prince whose wealth came from trade.

options.misconception: The portrait shows royal power, not submission — the scepter, crown, and warships say the king rules.
options.text: As a humble servant of Parliament.
As a warrior-king ruling by his own royal authority.

rationales.A: The armor, scepter, and crown are the marks of a king, not a merchant — the portrait is about royal power.
rationales.B: Nothing in the portrait bows to Parliament; the scepter, crown, and warships all say the king rules.
rationales.C: Armor, scepter, crown, and warships behind him — the portrait shows a king who rules by royal authority and force.
rationales.D: James never lived in America; he ruled the colonies from London, and the portrait was painted there.
rationales.general:
1. List what the painter shows. Armor, a scepter, a crown on a cushion, warships firing behind him.
2. Ask what those objects mean. Each one says power: the armor says war, the scepter says rule, the crown says kingship.
3. Ask what is missing. No Parliament, no assembly, no charter — nobody shares the frame with him.
4. Name the message. Background: James believed kings ruled by God's appointment, not by Parliament's leave. The portrait is that belief in paint.
Remember: a royal portrait is a claim about power, so read the objects like a sentence.

stimulus.source_note: Portrait from the shared image pool; Sir Godfrey Kneller, King James II (1684), public domain.
stimulus.text: King James II, painted by Sir Godfrey Kneller in 1684, a year before James took the throne. The king stands in polished armor, a scepter in his right hand, the crown resting on a cushion at his left. Behind him, warships fire their guns and an anchor leans at his feet. Two years after this portrait was painted, James created the Dominion of New England, revoking the charters of the colonies from Delaware to Maine and placing them under a single royal governor, Edmund Andros.
